div.p: The undersigned, minister ad interim of exterior relations of the United States of Venezuela, has received an order from the illustrious American, President of the Republic, to address the most excellent minister resident of the United States of North America, with the object which he proceeds to expound succinctly.

That legation knows that on the 17th of May last a new apportionment was made among the creditor governments of the funds of the thirteen per cent, destined to the payment of the diplomatic reclamations. Till then the distribution accorded on the 29th of July, 1873, had governed, which had a provisional character, whilst the respective credits were definitely liquidated, in order to fix the exact bases of the pro rata. The United States and Spain complained against this distribution, founding themselves in that it was not proportional to the amount of the respective credits. To remedy the inequality was the purpose of the determination of the 17th of May. That being communicated to the foreign diplomatic agents, those of France and Great Britain protested against it; and although the groundlessness of that step was demonstrated to them, they have excused themselves from entering into discussion. As disputes exist concerning the payment of interest, which in some cases has never been approved by the Congress, and in others has not even been stipulated, the government believed that if it took the base of the recognized capitals the unobjectionable (intachable) proportion would result. Thus it was done; but such good reasons have not been heeded.

The plenipotentiary of Venezuela at Paris and London has ventilated the matter with the Governments of France and Great Britain. Not only have these not accepted the said resolution, but they have exacted the fulfillment of the primitive conventions; which, if done, would leave the republic incapacitated to satisfy the other diplomatic conventions on credits of the same origin as those of these nations, and even to fulfill the necessities of its existence and improvements.

Finally M. Freycinet, minister of foreign affairs of France, called that of Venezuela to a conference, and in it manifested to him that his government did not mix itself in the interior combinations of this country, but that it could not accept a less quota than that assigned in 1873, and that such resolution was definitive; that if this was not acceded to, it would see itself in the condition (enel caso) to proceed in another manner, since, on the contrary, its position would be unsustainable before the chambers. Its chargé d’affaires has repeated the same words here, and has been made to know that Venezuela maintains the resolution of the 17th of May.

Although the government can hardly imagine that for a question of more or less monthly pecuniary quota the friendly relations of France should be disturbed, particularly when there exists there, and is becoming more and more established, the republican
form, preferred in America, it believes it proper to solicit the good offices of the United States to the end of preventing consequences which may present themselves.

The President of the Republic hopes that the President of the United States will vouchsafe to receive this solicitude with the interest which, to him, the fate of the Spanish-American Republics merits, and take a step whose good exit will assure his high influence and the consideration which he so justly enjoys in both worlds.
